item.title: 5 Ways to Take Control of Bipolar Disorder
item.description:
Bipolar Disorder

5 Ways to Take Control of Bipolar Disorder

A powerful lifestyle therapy can help prevent manic and depressive episodes.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • “Social rhythm therapy” is simple and often effective (and not a new dance step).
  • Identifying and managing daily life rhythms and triggers is up to you, and powerful.
  • Social rhythm therapy can help some people avoid or soften bipolar episodes.
Source: Ron Lach/Pexels

A bipolar diagnosis is a major life change, and as we learn more and more about the bipolar spectrum, we know bipolar II, and other less impactful versions than bipolar I, are more common than we think. And often, easier to control.

Although medication management is the hallmark of living well with bipolar, lifestyle hacks (like social rhythm therapy, or SRT) can be effective in helping forestall episodes or decreasing their intensity once they begin. Medications and therapy work best together—better than either alone—and SRT is a therapy that’s in your hands.

A simple lifestyle tool that can make a big difference, SRT is easy and just what it sounds like: paying attention to “social” rhythms and managing lifestyle triggers. Here’s how it works:

1. Sleep

You’ve probably heard this, but lack of sleep for even a day or two (or oversleeping on the other end) may tip you into hypomania, mania, or depression. Healthy sleep is essential to bipolar health, yet often complicated by the fact that bipolar people often have trouble sleeping to begin with. Pay attention to these tips:

  • Sleep rhythms are crucial to recovery. This doesn’t mean you have to go to bed and wake up at exactly the same time every day. But within an hour or so on each end is ideal. It’s nearly impossible to optimize daily moods in the short or long term if your brain can’t rely on regular sleep—and right amounts of it.
  • If you sense you’re revving up into hypomania or mania and can’t sleep, talk to your provider about a safe sleep aid to use rarely, just in case. Regular sleep, and sleep aids in times of disrupted sleep, can prevent many a full-blown manic or depressive episode from ever beginning.

Light

We know light exposure is critical to healthy humans in general, and people with bipolar disorder tend to be more sensitive to light cues. This means maximizing getting out into natural light, even for a few minutes walking from your car into work each morning. And in the evenings, keeping artificial lights low after sunset. Having morning light exposure helps your bipolar brain maintain stability and circadian rhythm. If you can’t get natural light, light therapy has been shown to be helpful in bipolar management, and often worth the small investment in a light box.

Exercise

When you’re outside for those few minutes soaking up natural light in the morning, bring your dog (or cat or ferret or bearded dragon) and take a walk. Use the “social” in social rhythm, and meet someone at the gym, keeping each other accountable. Maintaining a regular exercise rhythm (again, not exact, but simply regular), helps keep your brain and body stable, and increases the likelihood of healthy slumber after that workout.

Eating

Running on fumes and fried chicken, french fries, and funnel cake? Just like everything else, there’s time for that. But not each day. Your body needs healthy food, and regular intake. Skipping meals, then ravenously binging; eating late at night without time to digest; or relying on alcohol or other substances to sleep (or wake), messes up your mood stability. Keep trail mix or healthy snacks in your car, at work, and in your bag or purse. That way, when you realize you skipped a meal or won’t have dinner until late, you can eat healthy nutrients and improve your mood too.

Travel

Think about it. Humans have not had cars, trains, or planes for more than a second in evolutionary time. Moving from one time zone to another (let alone several) is not something our bodies were made for. It’s amazing we adjust as quickly as we do. And in bipolar disorder, traveling can be a major trigger. It’s not just time zone changes, but also disrupted sleep, routines, and schedules that accompany travel and mess with a steady mood. Prep your brain before and during travel. Focus on maintaining sleep, exercise, and light exposure as much as you can. Take an extra day if needed, to acclimate. Then, enjoy your trip.

Taking meds on time and on schedule, as well as knowing your unique triggers (and how to manage them) can be life-changing for those with bipolar disorder. You can find a simple bipolar mood chart online, and record these factors to get a sense of the best “social rhythm” for you. If you record even a week or two (OK, a month or more is better, but not required), you’ll likely look back at the chart and notice things you never knew about yourself. Making these connections between mood and daily rhythms is powerful and effective. And all in your hands.

item.title: What We Really Need When We're Hurting
item.description:
Emotions

What We Really Need When We're Hurting

Reasons why we stopped asking for comfort when we're hurting.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • Consolation is a relational act that changes how suffering is experienced, not whether it exists.
  • The emotional system signals pain as a call for connection, not a problem to be solved.
  • Productivity culture replaced comfort with validating, leaving a need that grows in silence when unmet.

There is a particular kind of emotional need that most people experience but few can describe. It appears after a breakup, during an illness, following a disappointment, or in the aftermath of a painful interaction. Sometimes it emerges when nothing dramatic has happened at all but the accumulation of life's ordinary hurts, or the ache of having been surprised by the unexpected words, actions, or silence of someone you care for.

The person may feel sad, discouraged, hurt, frightened, lonely, or overwhelmed. If you ask what they need, they often can't answer, and not because nothing is needed. Something very specific is needed: consolation. Yet as a concept, it has quietly disappeared from our shared vocabulary. We do not talk much about consolation anymore. And if we don't ask for it, the need grows in silence, becoming one of those unmet needs that leaves a mark without a name.

A woman lying down with a comforting hand on her shoulder, expressing support and care.
Source: Liza Summer/Pexels

The Decline of Consolation in Modern Culture

The word comes from the Latin consolari, to comfort, to soothe. For most of human history, consolation was considered one of the most important things one person could offer another. It had a place in philosophy, in literature, in religious practice, in the ordinary fabric of community life. Somewhere along the way, it lost its standing. Culture around emotional pain shifted in ways that made consolation harder to ask for, harder to give, and harder to even recognize as a legitimate response to suffering.

Several things contributed to this. The rise of psychotherapy and self-help culture gave us a new vocabulary for pain built around action: we process, reframe, validate, and work through. Useful ideas, but they carry an implicit message that the right response to emotional pain is to do something about it. Consolation doesn't do anything. It simply accompanies. Cognitive approaches reinforced this further, placing understanding at the center of emotional work; identifying patterns, reframing beliefs, or finding someone to blame became the gold standard of feeling better. And individualism did the rest. To ask for consolation may sound like an admission that you cannot carry the pain alone; a sign of emotional weakness in cultures that prize self-sufficiency. So we don't ask. We say we're fine, or we wait to see if someone notices without being told.

The person offering comfort faces a parallel pressure. Sitting with someone's pain without trying to fix it can feel passive, even irresponsible. We were simply never shown that staying, without fixing, is its own form of care.

The Science of Consolation: Why Presence Matters

And yet, what the science of emotion tells us is that presence is often exactly what is needed.

The need for consolation emerges whenever emotional pain exceeds what we can comfortably carry alone. We instinctively seek another person to help us bear its weight, and that instinct is the emotional system signaling that this pain belongs in the presence of another, that connection is what the moment requires. Psychologists call this co-regulation. Children demonstrate it openly. A newborn needs the caregiver's arms to soothe the pain of hunger, tiredness, and cold. A child who falls often begins looking for a parent before even assessing the injury. Not seeking medical expertise. Seeking comfort.

As adults, we continue to need the same thing but become less direct about it. Instead of saying "Please console me," we complain, withdraw, become irritable, or keep circling the same story. We only know that something inside us settles when another person is truly there; when we can lower our defenses, quiet our internal chatter, and rest in the presence of someone whose face says I'm here without needing to say a word.

In those moments, the emotional system is not asking for meaning-making or problem-solving. Those will come later. Right now, it is asking for something much simpler: a hug, a moment of warmth, someone sincere enough to lean into so the falling stops. Because what people need in those moments is not only to be validated; they need to be valued. Those are not the same thing.

Common Mistakes When Trying to Comfort Others

Now consider the other side; the one being asked to give something we were never quite taught to give. When someone we care about is suffering, most of us instinctively want to make the pain go away. We offer advice, suggest solutions, explain why things happened. Some of us, with the best intentions, say things like "it's not that bad" or "you'll be fine," which, however well-meaning, tells the person that what they are feeling is too much or in need of correction. This impulse comes from discomfort, not indifference; from helplessness, anxiety, or our own unresolved experiences.

Sticky notes on a whiteboard to find solutions
Source: Jakub Zerdzicki

But consolation does not require competence. It requires willingness. It is an act of dignity; an acknowledgment that suffering is part of being human and that emotional pain does not need to be corrected or removed in order to deserve care. The person in pain does not need to be fixed. They need to be met.

So, here is my recommendation: To those who tend to jump into fixing: consider offering the gift of your presence first. The solutions can wait. The person in front of you usually cannot.

To those who are hurting and hoping someone will understand: you are allowed to ask for comfort. Naming what you need is not weakness. It is how we let others in.

item.title: The Missing Secret Ingredient of Self-Help Advice
item.description:
Self-Help

The Missing Secret Ingredient of Self-Help Advice

What's missing from self-help advice? Ironically, it’s the self.

Posted June 15, 2026

Key points
  • The general formula for self-help advice involves some people telling other people what worked for them.
  • Trying to follow someone else's advice is not "self"-help.
  • If what works for others doesn’t work for you, that’s because their way is not your way.

The late, great American comedian George Carlin once joked, “I went to a bookstore and asked the saleswoman, 'Where's the self-help section?' She said if she told me, it would defeat the purpose.” While Carlin’s gag can be thought of as just a bit of fun, it also provides a shrewd comment on the state of self-help.

The self-help industry is monstrous. There are books, podcasts, workshops, apps, retreats, Facebook groups, and other ways of advising what people can do to improve themselves, reach their potential, achieve inner contentment, and so on. Some self-help books sell millions of copies so, clearly, loads of people want to make their lives better.

I’ve read a lot of self-help books. From my reading, I've noticed a pattern. First, someone describes a time when things were seriously awful. Then, while they were floundering about in the basement of rock-bottom, they realized, thought, or did something that profoundly turned things around. Next, as their life becomes more incredible than they thought possible, they write a book about all the wonderfulness the turnaround thingamajig brought them.

Later, their book sells millions of copies as others rush to use the turnaround tactic in their own lives. The creator and author of the turnaround doohickey is then invited to give talks to large audiences and appear on TV. They might even start their own website and podcast.

Why Others’ Solutions Might Not Work For You

For me, it’s inspirational every time I learn of another unique and crafty way that someone managed to propel themselves out of misery and mayhem. The key point, though, is that they propelled themselves. I've never read a self-help book where someone describes trying out another person’s strategy and have it give them the same gloriousness that it brought the creator.

There's nothing wrong at all with people sharing their success stories. But there is a problem in assuming that one person’s solution will be the answer for others. This is a problem because people might think that if a solution works well for others but doesn’t work for them, then that must mean there is something wrong with them.

A much greater appreciation that your way is not my way would help. If someone else’s ideas don’t work for you, that doesn’t mean there’s anything wrong with you. It just means that those suggestions aren't a good fit for you and the life you’re living.

But don’t stop being interested in other people’s success. On the contrary, if you’re on a self-improvement quest, read as widely as you can. There’s a self-help feast out there. Devour whatever grabs your attention. Dive into it with gusto, but shake it off just as quickly if it doesn’t put wind under your wings.

Choosing Whether to Pursue Self-Help

And, of course, it’s completely fine not to jump on the self-help bandwagon. Maybe you’re satisfied with the way things are and the direction you’re heading. That’s tremendous. In fact, that’s probably the state of mind that those who become self-helpists want to achieve.

All of the self-help books could be thought of as case studies of what’s possible.

More than anything, self-help books show the extraordinarily audacious tenacity of the human spirit. We really can overcome the most outrageous obstacles.

So, an important message from these books is about what can be achieved regardless of how horrible and hopeless things might be. But all happy endings are uniquely individual.

Read all you want about what other people have done but remember, the how of bringing success your way is a recipe only you can make.

When you think about it, following someone else’s advice isn’t really self-help. We need to put the self back into self-help. My way is not your way. I can help you find your way, but I can’t give it to you, and I can’t find it for you. Only you can create it, and only you will know it when it arrives.

Source: Timothy Carey

Why Understanding Yourself Is Vital for Self-Improvement

The starting point for self-improvement must be the self. Getting to know as much of yourself as you can will help you better understand why things are the way they are, and where and what your point of inspiration might be.

Will you recognize your turnaround doodad when it comes along? Is it already here but you’re not paying attention to it? What’s currently running through your mind? No, not those things. The other things. Those frisky little ideas that briefly appear then scamper away. What happens if you start catching them? They’re yours too. What do they tell you about you?

It’s simply a fact that no-one else can do self-help for you. Lots of things can help but nothing can replace you in the driver’s seat. Perhaps the first step in genuine, lasting, ideal self-help, is realizing that it’s the self and only the self that takes not just the first one, but all the steps that follow.

Where might your stepping take you?
